source.title: HiddenDetect: Detecting Jailbreak Attacks against Large Vision-Language Models via Monitoring Hidden States
source.authors: Yi-Lei Jiang; Xinyan Gao; Tian-Shuo Peng; Ying-Shui Tan; Xiao-Yong Zhu; Bo Zheng; Xiang-Yu Yue

record.tranche_reason: The study uses refusal-related hidden-state signals to build a jailbreak detector and reports detector and activation results, but it does not intervene on the difference-in-means residual-stream direction or test the claim versions about that direction.
record.gate_note: The paper measures cosine alignment between hidden states and a sparse refusal-token vector, and reports harmful-versus-safe activation patterns and weight-scaling results. Figure 2 values are used to select layers and are not recorded. Table 1 detector comparisons and Table 2 detector ablations report the performance of the paper's new method, not what the claim's direction itself does, so they are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study builds a jailbreak detector from cosine similarity between logit-lens-projected hidden states and a sparse refusal-token vocabulary vector. It never computes a difference-in-means residual-stream direction and never ablates or adds one. Its weight-scaling ablation scales whole layers and counts over-rejections, which is not a test of a single direction. The activation analyses measure a refusal-token alignment score, a related but different construct. These are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that LVLM hidden states carry refusal-related signals that a training-free detector (HiddenDetect) can exploit; it beats baseline detectors on AUROC. The signals are delayed and weaker for visually conveyed harm. Bimodal safety alignment strengthens them mainly for cross-modal queries.
record.recipe_differences: The paper constructs a sparse vocabulary-space vector from refusal tokens and measures cosine alignment with projected hidden states, including an unsafe-minus-safe discrepancy. It does not use the original difference-in-means residual-stream direction or perform the original causal ablation/addition interventions.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported refusal activation patterns vary by query type and modality; cross-modal safety activation is described as delayed and diminished relative to harmful-text queries. Bimodal safety alignment changes cross-modal activation more than harmful-text activation. Weight-scaling rejection counts vary with layer range and scaling factor.

fits_no_version.finding: In LLaVA-v1.5-7b, the refusal-token alignment discrepancy is weaker and arrives later in depth for image-grounded harmful queries than for harmful text. Crafted jailbreak text and image pairing also lower it.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In LVLMs, refusal-related hidden-state signals emerge later and more weakly when harmful intent is conveyed visually.

fits_no_version.finding: Bimodal safety alignment raises refusal-token alignment mainly for cross-modal harmful queries and leaves harmful-text queries nearly unchanged.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Bimodal safety alignment strengthens refusal-related signals for cross-modal harmful queries more than for text queries.

fits_no_version.finding: Scaling the weights of layers 16–29 by 1.1–1.2 raises rejections of benign bimodal queries from 33 to as many as 49.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Up-scaling mid-to-late layer weights in LVLMs increases over-refusal on benign multimodal inputs.

fits_no_version.finding: Projections onto the refusal-token vector separate toxic from benign samples most at layers 22–24. The final layer shows inconsistencies.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Separation along refusal-token semantics varies by layer in LVLMs.

record.problems: The layer-selection analysis uses a small few-shot set. Several relevant activation results are presented as plots without numerical values or uncertainty estimates. The weight-scaling study reports rejection counts for benign queries but does not state the sample count in the main text. The study does not test causal mediation by the claimed direction or assess general capability after such an intervention.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1 (Section 5.2) reports AUROC for HiddenDetect and comparison methods, and Table 2 (Section 5.3) reports detector ablations; these are evaluations of the paper's detector rather than outcomes of the claimed direction. Figure 2 (Section 3.3) is used to select the most safety-aware layers, so its values are not included.

untested.parts: No difference-in-means direction is computed. No directional ablation or addition is run, and capability is not checked after any intervention.
No weight orthogonalization is applied. The layer weight scaling multiplies whole layers and is not abliteration.
The study does not suppress the direction during jailbreaks or train against its ablation. It only reports that jailbreak text lowers its refusal-token alignment score.
No comparison of single-direction, affine or cone accounts.
Harmfulness and refusal are not separated.
Cross-modal and alignment comparisons use the refusal-token score, not transfer of a difference-in-means direction.
The before/after bimodal alignment comparison uses the refusal-token score and does not test whether a removable direction exists.

record.verdict_notes: Arditi et al. is cited only as prior work. The 'refusal vector' here is a binary vector over refusal tokens in vocabulary space, not the claim's residual-stream direction. Table 3 does not give the sample count. For r14, α=1.2 on layers 16–22 gives 39, one fewer than α=1.1. That conflicts with the caption's claim that higher α leads to more rejections.

versions.untested_parts: No difference-in-means residual-stream direction is ablated or added; refusal behavior and preservation of general capability after such interventions are not tested.
No ablation is converted into a weight edit to remove refusals.
The study does not suppress the claimed direction in attacks or train models against its ablation.
Layerwise activation patterns are measured, but the study does not compare a single direction with an affine, cone, or multi-direction account of refusal.
Harmfulness judgments and refusal decisions are not separately measured.
The study evaluates detectors on several LVLMs, but does not test whether the claimed direction transfers across languages, model variants, or base-to-instruct models.
The study compares activation strength before and after bimodal safety alignment, but does not test how training determines whether a single removable direction exists.
